summary:
Space Weather can create disastrous events that would take down Earth's man made structures such as power grids,  satellites, GPS  yet the warning is a complex chart only an expert can read. We believe in accessibility and simplicity, so we made it something you can understand visually as well as hear clearly. 

What we built: Heliophon turns live NASA DONKI, NOAA SWPC/GOES and Kyoto WDC data into a living soundscape: five continuous layers (Kp, flare class, Dst, CME speed, proton flux) and five alerts for grid, GPS, satellite, radiation and radio risk, beside a solar system view and Earth magnetosphere inset. Replay Quebec 1989 in Simulation mode.

Relevance: Sound is the interface, not an afterthought to a chart. It’s NASA and NOAA data you can listen to.

Impact: Space weather threatens grids, GPS, satellites and aviation radio, but warnings are mostly visual. Heliophon reaches blind and low-vision users and operators whose eyes are busy.

Creativity: Simple by design: one sound per physical driver, so the meaning lives in the sound itself.

Validity: Real, attributed data. Live and simulated modes are clearly labeled, and the sound is a design choice, not an official warning.

Heliophon. See the Sun & hear the Sun.
details:
Heliophon: hear the Sun.

What it does and how it works
Heliophon pulls live space weather data from NASA DONKI, NOAA SWPC/GOES and Kyoto WDC and turns it into sound with Tone.js. Once you press Play, five layers run continuously: a bass drone driven by the Kp index, a lead tone for GOES flare class, a sub-bass rumble for Dst, a two-tone siren for CME speed, and filtered noise for proton flux. Five threshold-triggered alerts (grid blackout, GPS disruption, satellite drag, radiation risk, comms blackout) add distinct sounds when conditions cross their limits, and they are debounced to avoid alarm fatigue. The screen shows what you hear: a solar system view with a CME cone, an Earth inset with magnetosphere and aurora ovals, a live waveform, and a red alert banner for G3+ watches. A Simulation mode replays historical storms such as Quebec 1989 through the same engine.

Benefits and intended impact
Space weather can disrupt power grids, GPS, satellites and aviation radio, but warnings mostly live in charts and feeds. Heliophon makes them accessible to blind and low-vision users and lets operators stay aware without watching a screen. It runs in any browser with no install or account. We hope it makes space weather easier to follow and more inclusive, as a complement to official warnings, never a replacement.

Tools and technology
Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Tone.js (Web Audio API), deployed as a static export on Vercel. Data: NASA DONKI, NOAA SWPC/GOES, Kyoto WDC, with a 20-minute local cache. No special hardware, only a browser and speakers or headphones.

Creativity
Sound is the interface, not a chart sonified afterward. Each sound maps to one physical driver, and meaning comes from timbre and familiar warning cues (sirens, descending glides, minor chords) rather than melodies to learn.

What we considered
Accessibility: screen-reader support, ARIA live alerts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, and audio that starts only on user action. Honesty: attributed data, clearly labeled simulation, and a plain statement that the sound is a design choice, not an official warning. Reliability: caching to respect API rate limits, and a visible cached-data badge when offline. Simplicity: no backend and no setup. We believe in accessibility and simplicity.
